clue.text: Irksome to catch terrible ruler time travelling for fun

indicators.note: to catch means the irksome word holds the other pieces within it

parts.note: something irksome is galling
Ivan the Terrible, the Russian tsar

explanation.surface: An annoying despot who keeps time-travelling for amusement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to catch' signals the insertion; Ivan the Terrible is the crossword's stock terrible ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallivanting is roaming about in search of pleasure or entertainment.

clue.text: One tickled extremely graceful royal behind carriage

indicators.note: behind means the following pieces come after the carriage in this down answer

parts.note: a gig is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage

indicators.note: extremely picks the two extreme letters of graceful

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for a royal

explanation.surface: A very elegant royal riding behind in a carriage is amused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' and 'behind' are the signals; 'One tickled' is a person who laughs, not someone being touched.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tickled is amused, and a giggler is one who laughs at it.

clue.text: Pope with curse about clingy garment

parts.note: Leo is the name of many popes

indicators.note: about means the curse word is turned round

parts.note: drat is a mild curse

explanation.surface: A pope swears over a tight-fitting item of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns DRAT into TARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A leotard is a close-fitting one-piece garment worn by dancers and gymnasts.

clue.text: Forced into service, Buccaneer has to hurry

parts.note: Buccaneer is the setter's pseudonym, so the setter says I'm (I am)
someone pressed for time has to hurry

explanation.surface: A pirate is press-ganged and must rush.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is Buccaneer, so 'Buccaneer' gives I'M. 'Forced into service' recalls the navy's press gangs.
explanation.definitionFit: To impress is to conscript men into the navy or army by force, as press gangs did.

clue.text: Disconcert leader of air strike

indicators.note: leader of picks the opening letter of air

parts.note: to bash is to strike hard

explanation.surface: The head of an air attack aims to unsettle the enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash is to make someone embarrassed or disconcerted.

clue.text: Fix diet, getting mashed bananas now

indicators.note: mashed means crushed, so the letters of diet are rearranged
bananas means crazy, so the letters of now are muddled

explanation.surface: A dieter fixes on mashed bananas now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mashed' turns DIET into TIED and 'bananas' turns NOW into OWN. 'Bananas' looks like the fruit but is the madness signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To tie down something is to secure it firmly in place.

clue.text: Hill rising for all to see above oddly leaden clouds

indicators.note: above means the earlier pieces sit over the last in this down answer
rising in a down clue means the hill word reads upwards

parts.note: ben is a Scottish word for a mountain or hill
U is the British film certificate meaning suitable for all audiences

indicators.note: oddly picks the first, third and fifth letters of leaden

explanation.surface: A hill rises in full view above grey, lead-coloured clouds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns BEN into NEB; 'oddly' gives LAE from leaden.
explanation.definitionFit: Nebulae are vast interstellar clouds of gas and dust.

clue.text: Little Queen Victoria, say, welcomes assistance

parts.note: mini means small

indicators.note: welcomes means the station takes the queen letter inside

parts.note: London Victoria is a railway station, an example
R, for Regina, stands for queen

explanation.surface: Little Queen Victoria accepts some help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcomes' puts R inside STATION. 'Victoria' looks like the queen but is the London terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: Ministration is the giving of help or care, as in ministering to the sick.

clue.text: Voguish women ejected from mature clique

parts.note: voguish means fashionable, in

indicators.note: ejected from means the women's letter is thrown out of the word for mature

parts.note: to mature is to grow up

explanation.surface: Fashionable women are thrown out of a grown-up social set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ejected from' removes W from GROW UP, leaving GROUP.
explanation.definitionFit: An in-group is an exclusive set of insiders, which is what a clique is.

clue.text: Old-fashioned retort discombobulated male writer

indicators.note: discombobulated means confused, so the letters of male are jumbled

parts.note: a Bic is a brand of ballpoint pen, a writer

explanation.surface: A confused man responds with an outdated comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discombobulated' turns MALE into ALEM. 'Retort' looks like a sharp reply but is the chemist's distilling vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: An alembic is an antique distilling apparatus, a kind of retort used by alchemists.

clue.text: Official is going both ways, hugged by man in the street?

indicators.note: hugged by means the doubled word is held inside the ordinary man

parts.note: an ordinary person, a commoner

indicators.note: going both ways means the word is is written forwards then backwards

parts.note: is forwards then reversed

explanation.surface: A bisexual official is embraced by an ordinary passer-by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going both ways' reads the word forwards then backwards, ISSI; 'hugged by' signals the insertion. The surface plays on the slang sense of going both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: A commissioner is an official in charge of a government department or body.

clue.text: Current case for lay-off accepted by weak, bad rep

parts.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current

indicators.note: accepted by means the case letters go inside the word for weak

parts.note: lame means weak, as a lame excuse

indicators.note: case for means the outside letters of lay-off are taken

explanation.surface: A worker facing redundancy who is feeble earns a poor reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case for' picks L and F from lay-off; 'accepted by' puts them inside LAME, giving LLFAME after I.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill fame is a poor reputation, as in a house of ill fame; rep is short for reputation.

clue.text: Crook's loud partying in residence, dropping ecstasy

definitions.note: read as 'Crook is', so the definition is the noun crook and 's links it

indicators.note: in means the jumbled letters sit inside the trimmed home
dropping means the ecstasy letter is left out of the residence word

parts.note: a residence is a home
E is the common abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: partying suggests letters let loose and rearranged

explanation.surface: A criminal throws a noisy party at home but goes without the drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' leaves HOM; 'partying' gives ODLU, which 'in' places within.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoodlum is a thug or gangster, a synonym for a criminal.

clue.text: Overworked painter finally drew borders

indicators.note: borders means the word for drew surrounds the picked letter

parts.note: teams that drew tied the match

indicators.note: finally picks the closing letter of painter

explanation.surface: An exhausted artist ends up sketching picture frames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives R from painter; 'borders' has TIED around it. 'Drew' looks like sketching but means drawing a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone overworked is worn out, exhausted from too much effort.

clue.text: Place, one around green ground in national park

indicators.note: around means the place word wraps the scrambled letters

parts.note: to place something is to set it

indicators.note: ground as in ground up, so the letters of green are crushed into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone sets things down around the ground of a national park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' gives ERENG and 'around' wraps the place word about it. 'Place' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti in Tanzania is one of Africa's best-known national parks.

clue.text: In theatre, removal of clothing for rude part

indicators.note: clothing for means the outer letters of rude, which clothe it, are taken

parts.note: a section is a part

explanation.surface: A stage show removes costumes for a lewd scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothing for' picks R and E from rude. 'In theatre' means the operating theatre, not the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A resection is the surgical removal of part of an organ, done in an operating theatre.

clue.text: Poles from Poland wanting land in Barking instead

indicators.note: in means the cut-down Poland goes inside the jumbled letters
barking means mad, so the letters of instead go crazy
wanting means lacking, so the letters of land are removed from Poland

explanation.surface: Polish people arrive from Poland seeking land in the London suburb of Barking instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting' leaves the first two letters of Poland; 'Barking' gives ANTIDES and 'in' places within. Barking is a district of east London, and 'Poles' is the definition, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipodes are diametrically opposite points on the globe, as the two poles are.

clue.text: Old writer briefly tucks into one drink or another

indicators.note: tucks into means the shortened pen goes inside the drink

parts.note: tea is one drink

indicators.note: briefly means the old writer is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: a quill is an old-fashioned pen

explanation.surface: An elderly author helps himself to one drink after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' and 'tucks into' are the signals; 'tucks into' sounds like eating.
explanation.definitionFit: Tequila is a second drink set against the first, a spirit distilled from agave.

clue.text: Lady, second to none, shedding pounds

indicators.note: shedding means the pound letter is cast off

parts.note: peerless means unequalled, second to none
L, from libra, is the abbreviation for pounds sterling

explanation.surface: An unrivalled woman loses weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shedding' takes L from PEERLESS. 'Pounds' looks like weight but is money.
explanation.definitionFit: A peeress is a woman holding a peerage, entitled to be called Lady.

clue.text: M&S skirts mostly available for Eeyorish people

indicators.note: skirts means the M and S go round the outside, like a skirt

parts.note: M&S supplies its two letters M and S

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: available means open, as a job open to applicants

explanation.surface: Marks & Spencer's skirts are mostly on sale for gloomy shoppers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' and 'skirts' are the signals. M&S is Marks & Spencer, a British chain store; Eeyore is the gloomy donkey in Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.definitionFit: Mopes are listless, melancholy people, just like the downcast donkey Eeyore.

clue.text: Ace communist leader snatching rest at work

indicators.note: snatching means the leader grabs the reworked letters inside him

parts.note: Mao Zedong led communist China

indicators.note: at work means the letters of rest are put to work in a new order

explanation.surface: A top-notch communist chairman grabs a break while working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at work' gives ESTR and 'snatching' puts the leader around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a master of an art, someone who is an ace at it.

clue.text: Rears about to be covered by underwear

indicators.note: to be covered by means the short word is wrapped inside the underwear

parts.note: pants are underwear in British English
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Backsides are about to be covered with underpants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be covered by' signals the insertion. 'Rears' looks like backsides but is the verb to bring up.
explanation.definitionFit: To parent a child is to raise or bring it up, so parents as a verb means rears.

clue.text: In Spain, what stops this month's legal process

indicators.note: stops means the Spanish word plugs the gap within the abbreviation

parts.note: inst, short for instant, means of this month in old business letters
que is Spanish for what

explanation.surface: In Spain, something halts this month's court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stops' signals insertion, as a stopper plugs a hole; inst is old commercial shorthand for this month.
explanation.definitionFit: An inquest is a judicial inquiry, such as a coroner's investigation into a death.

clue.text: Carry on Matron's opening? It has symbolic value

parts.note: to tote is to carry

indicators.note: opening means the first letter of Matron's is taken

explanation.surface: A nod to the British comedy film Carry On Matron and its opening.
explanation.walkthrough: Carry On Matron is one of the long-running British Carry On film comedies.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is an object or emblem revered as a symbol of a clan or group.

clue.text: No end of cereal and toast

indicators.note: no end of means the final letter is removed from the cereal

parts.note: Cheerios is a brand of breakfast cereal

explanation.surface: Endless cereal and toast for breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' removes S from CHEERIOS. 'Toast' is not bread but a salute with drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerio can be said when raising a glass, a toast like cheers, as well as a farewell.

clue.text: Scot returned garment greener than the rest

indicators.note: returned means the Scottish name is sent back, read in reverse

parts.note: Ian is a typical Scottish man's name
a vest is a garment

explanation.surface: A Scotsman sends back an item of clothing that is greener than the others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns IAN into NAI. 'Greener' looks like colour but means more inexperienced.
explanation.definitionFit: Green means inexperienced or gullible, so the most green is the most innocent and credulous.

clue.text: Heated home maybe perfect

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
the perfect is an example of a grammatical tense

explanation.surface: A warm house may be ideal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' is not flawless but the grammatical perfect tense.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated argument is an intense one, full of passion.

clue.text: Tight, religious clothes are cut by simple fellow

indicators.note: clothes means the religious word wraps around the rest, dressing it

parts.note: pious means devoutly religious

indicators.note: cut means the final letter of are is snipped off

parts.note: Simple Simon of the nursery rhyme

explanation.surface: Devout outfits are slashed by a naive man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' trims the last letter and 'clothes' signals the religious word going round the rest; Simple Simon is the nursery-rhyme simpleton.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight means stingy with money, and parsimonious means extremely unwilling to spend.
